prompt: Some people believe that university education should be free for everyone, regardless of their financial background. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
It is often argued that higher education should be provided free of charge to all students, irrespective of their financial circumstances. While I agree that university education should be accessible to people from disadvantaged backgrounds, I do not believe that making it entirely free for everyone is the most effective approach.

One major argument in favour of free university education is that it can promote equality of opportunity. Students from low-income families may possess considerable academic ability but be unable to afford tuition fees. If higher education were free, these individuals would have a greater chance of obtaining professional qualifications and improving their future career prospects. This could also benefit society as a whole, since countries would be able to develop a larger pool of highly educated workers in fields such as medicine, engineering and education.

However, providing free university education to everyone would place a substantial financial burden on governments. Public funds are limited, and money allocated to universities could otherwise be spent on essential services such as healthcare, public transport and primary education. Furthermore, wealthy families are generally capable of paying tuition fees themselves, meaning that universal free education could result in public money being used to subsidise people who do not actually need financial assistance. A more practical solution would therefore be to offer scholarships, grants or reduced fees to students from disadvantaged backgrounds while requiring those who can afford it to contribute towards the cost of their education.

In addition, charging reasonable tuition fees may encourage students to take their studies more seriously. When individuals make a financial investment in their education, they may be more motivated to attend classes, complete their coursework and graduate on time. Nevertheless, tuition fees should not be so high that they discourage capable students from poorer families from entering university.

In conclusion, although free university education can improve social mobility and provide greater equality of opportunity, I believe that making it universally free is neither financially sustainable nor necessary. A system in which financially disadvantaged students receive substantial government support, while those who can afford tuition contribute to the cost, would be a fairer and more sustainable alternative.
